expectations.text: Identifies the study as Terrell et al., PeerJ Computer Science 3:e111 (2017), covering 3,064,667 pull requests
expectations.evidence: "The source is Terrell et al., *"Gender differences and bias in open source: pull request acceptance of women versus men"* (PeerJ Computer Science 3:e111, 2017, DOI 10.7717/peerj-cs.111) — 3,064,667 pull requests analyzed, with gender inferred for 35.3% of users via name/Google+ linkage."

expectations.text: Confirms the 78.7% versus 74.6% figures describe the overall population, not the population this contribution path serves
expectations.evidence: "78.7% vs 74.6% is the overall, aggregate acceptance rate — insiders and outsiders mixed together. That's the wrong slice to answer 'is there a bias problem in how we review outside contributions'..."

expectations.text: Gives the restricted figures for outside contributors with an identifiable gender: women 58% against men 61%
expectations.evidence: "Restricted to outside contributors with an identifiable gender — the exact population your good-first-issue queue and cold-review process serve — women's merge rate drops to 58% against men's 61%. Lower, not higher."

expectations.text: Notes that contributors whose profiles were gender-neutral had the highest merge rate of all
expectations.evidence: "Contributors whose profiles were gender-neutral scored highest of all (70% women, 65% men) — i.e., when identity isn't visible, judgment is closer to pure merit..."

expectations.text: States the caveats: gender was inferred, only 35.3% of users were linkable, and the study predates many platform changes
expectations.evidence: "gender was inferred, not self-reported, only 35.3% of users were linkable, and this is 2017 data on a platform that's changed since."

expectations.text: Says the direction is robust while the exact percentages are not
expectations.evidence: "Treat the *direction* (outside-contribution bias against identifiably-female contributors, mitigated when identity is invisible) as robust; don't defend the exact percentages as precise."

expectations.text: Concludes that 'therefore there is no bias problem' does not follow, because the reversal appears exactly on outside contributions
expectations.evidence: "The pushback took the number that reflects the first fact and used it to deny the second, which is the opposite of what the paper's authors did with their own data." combined with the restricted-figure reversal specific to outside contributors

expectations.text: Prescribes reviewing against the written scope rule and the fixed review order rather than against an impression of the person, as the cheapest available control
expectations.evidence: "Review against a written scope rule and a fixed order, never against an impression of the contributor... This is the cheapest available control on reviewer bias precisely because it removes the reviewer's read of *who* submitted the patch from the decision path."

expectations.text: Notes the project needs a published scope rule and a fixed review order for that control to exist at all
expectations.evidence: "if Halyard doesn't already have a written scope statement and a fixed review order that maintainers actually follow, build that now — it's the direct, evidence-backed response to 'contributor diversity'"

expectations.text: Raises information-foraging cost - having to hunt for the process - as unevenly distributed across newcomers, citing the GenderMag work on cognitive-style barriers
